title: Why did cities grow between the Tigris and Euphrates?
answer: Mesopotamia was a region around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. In its drier southern lands, people dug channels to bring river water to their fields. Farming could support people who did other work, such as potters, builders, and traders. Some settlements grew into cities. Mud from the plains could be shaped into bricks and dried, so people built with a material they could find close to home. The region included many different peoples and governments over thousands of years.

title: What made Uruk one of the earliest cities?
answer: Uruk grew in southern Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago. Thousands of people could live near one another there. Large mud-brick buildings took more work to plan and build than a single family could handle. People who grew food worked alongside people who made pots, traded, or kept accounts. Some of the oldest tablets found at Uruk count goods. Details such as those help archaeologists see a city working, even though they cannot hear what people said in its streets.

title: What was the city of Ur?
answer: Ur was a large city in southern Mesopotamia. One of its best-known buildings was a ziggurat with stepped levels that rose above the flat ground. Three stairways rose toward the entrance on the front. The surviving outer brickwork helps archaeologists study how older builders made a huge structure from layers of material. Graves and everyday objects at Ur offer other clues about life there. A tall building tells us about organized labor, while a small object can tell us about someone’s work or habits.
facts: A ruler named Ur-Nammu began the great ziggurat at Ur about four thousand years ago.

title: How did Babylon become a great ancient city?
answer: Babylon stood on the Euphrates River in what is now Iraq. It was a center of power more than once. Under the Neo-Babylonian rulers, it had tall city walls and a grand road for ceremonies. One entrance called the Ishtar Gate was decorated with pictures of animals in glazed brick. The walls directed people entering the city, while the gate showed what its builders could do. Ruins and objects give us a clearer picture of Babylon than legends alone.

answer: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon who had rulings carved into a tall dark stone almost four thousand years ago. The small wedge marks give examples of disputes and punishments. title: How did the ancient Persian Empire govern faraway lands?
answer: The Achaemenid kings ruled an empire that stretched from Egypt and western Asia toward the Indus region. A king could not visit every town to decide what should happen there. Officials governed regions and answered to the king. The empire included people with many languages and local customs. Carvings from Persepolis show groups bringing objects from different lands. title: What was Persepolis built to show?

They raised stone columns above it and decorated stairs with lines of carved figures. The figures carry items or wear clothes that mark different places. The setting, size, and art helped show the power of the Persian kings and the many lands they claimed as part of their empire.

title: How did Carthage become a sea power?
answer: Carthage began as a settlement founded by Phoenician seafarers on the North African shore, near modern Tunis. A harbor close to routes across the Mediterranean made it a useful place to trade. From Carthage, ships could connect towns on both the African and European sides of the sea. As Carthage grew, it became powerful in its own right and fought Rome. Rome destroyed the older city in 146 BCE, then later built a Roman city at the same site.

title: What do city streets tell us about the Indus civilization?
answer: The Indus civilization grew in South Asia thousands of years ago. Today archaeologists study cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa to learn how people there lived. At Mohenjo-daro, some streets followed long straight lines, and many buildings used bricks. Covered drains carried water away from some homes and streets. Small carved seals show pictures of animals and lines of signs. Archaeologists can describe these objects and streets, but there is no agreed reading of the signs yet.

answer: The Shang dynasty ruled parts of northern China more than three thousand years ago. Its craftspeople made large bronze containers with carefully shaped patterns. Archaeologists also found animal bones and turtle shells with writing carved on them. Some record questions that rulers asked about the weather or harvests. Old stories about the Shang were written down much later. The objects are especially useful because people made and used them at the time those rulers lived.

title: What were oracle bones used for?

title: Why did people build the Great Wall of China?
answer: Rulers in different periods built walls, gates, and towers along parts of China’s northern frontier. Walls could slow a raid and guide people toward guarded crossings. title: What changed in China during the Han dynasty?
answer: The Han dynasty ruled for about four hundred years, with an interruption, after the Qin. Government officers kept written records and helped run provinces far from the main cities. title: Why do people call many routes the Silk Roads?
answer: The Silk Roads were linked routes between parts of Asia and places farther west. Travelers could choose different roads depending on the season, water, or who controlled a pass. A merchant often took a load only as far as the next town or market. Another person might carry it on from there. Silk was one famous trade good, but travelers also brought new ideas, stories, foods, and ways of making things. Exchange could continue even when particular routes became hard to use.

answer: Kush was a kingdom farther up the Nile from Egypt, in what is now Sudan. People there built towns, temples, and burial places. title: How did the ancient Maya organize their cities?
answer: Ancient Maya people built cities across parts of what are now Mexico and Central America. Each city and the lands around it could have its own ruler. Rulers built temples and palaces around open spaces and had writers record dates and events. Neighboring cities might trade or form friendships, then compete or fight at other times. answer: Ancient Maya writing used signs called glyphs. A glyph might stand for a whole word, or it might stand for a sound like the beginning of a word. Different signs can fit into one block. title: What is the Electoral College?
answer: When people vote for president of the United States, their votes help decide which group of electors their state will pick. Those electors cast formal votes for president and vice president later. States have different numbers of electors based on their representation in Congress, and the District of Columbia also has electors. In most states the winning candidate gets all of that state’s electoral votes. A candidate needs more than half of the electoral votes to win in the usual process.
facts: The Electoral College has 538 elector positions under the present allocation.

title: What does a jury do in a trial?
answer: A trial jury is a small group of people chosen to hear testimony and look at evidence in a court case. The judge tells them what legal rules to use. In a typical jury trial, the group discusses the facts and gives a decision called a verdict. Some trial juries decide whether a person has been proved guilty of a crime. Others settle disputes between people or organizations. Courts can also decide many cases without a jury.
facts: In the federal system, a grand jury asks a different question from a trial jury, about whether a criminal charge can go forward.

title: What do state and local governments do?
answer: In the United States, states make many rules for people and organizations within their state. Cities, towns, and counties may handle work that affects smaller places, such as collecting trash or taking care of local streets. The exact work depends on the state and the community. A school board, city council, or county office might decide different things. In many places voters choose some of these local officials. Other people are hired or appointed to do work for the community.

facts: Depending on where you live, local elections can include city, county, or school offices.

title: What can a town decide at a town meeting?
answer: In some towns, a town meeting makes certain local decisions. People might talk about how much the town should spend or whether a town rule needs to change. An open meeting can let registered town voters vote for themselves. Other towns elect representatives who do the voting at the meeting. A moderator helps the meeting follow its rules while people speak and vote. The meeting’s work depends on state law and how the town is organized.
facts: Massachusetts has towns with both open and representative town meetings.

title: What happens to ballots in an election?
answer: Officials set up an election so eligible voters can choose among candidates or answer questions on a ballot. Depending on where they live, people might vote at a voting place or return a ballot by mail. After people have voted, election workers count valid ballots and check records. They may compare totals, review ballots whose choices are unclear, and perform other required checks. Officials announce and confirm results after following the rules for that election, which can differ by state.
facts: In the United States, many elections are run by local officials under state rules.

title: What does it mean to become a citizen by naturalization?
answer: A citizen is someone recognized as a member of a country under its laws. Some people are citizens at birth. A person who becomes a citizen after birth can sometimes do so through a legal process called naturalization. In the United States the process can include an application, an interview, and an oath at a ceremony. Different rules can apply to people with different histories. New citizens can take part in civic life and may vote if they meet the voting rules.

facts: Naturalization and citizenship at birth are different ways a person can become a citizen.

title: How can two different languages be related?
answer: Languages can change a little as people pass them on. Groups sometimes move apart and use language in different ways, generation after generation. After a long time, the groups may speak languages that no longer sound much alike. Linguists compare patterns in older words and sounds to look for shared beginnings. English, German, and Spanish are different languages in a large family called Indo-European. Comparing a whole pattern is more helpful than finding just one word that happens to sound alike.

facts: Two languages can be related even when someone who speaks one cannot understand the other.

title: Why do people use the same language in different ways?
answer: A dialect is a form of a language used by a group of people. Their words, pronunciation, or ways of putting words together can differ from another group’s. One person might say “soda” where another says “pop.” People learn features from family, friends, books, and the places they spend time. A dialect has patterns its speakers learn, even when those patterns differ from the way a textbook speaks. Groups can share some features and differ in others.
aliases: why do people say words differently
facts: An accent describes pronunciation. A dialect can also differ in words or grammar.

title: How can a prefix or suffix change a word?
answer: Some words have parts that help you guess the meaning. The beginning part in “rewrite” is re-, which often means again. The last part of “helpful” is -ful, which helps show that something gives or has help. English uses many parts that cannot stand alone as words. Looking for a familiar part may help you understand a new word, but the whole word often has a more specific meaning. Check how it is used in the sentence.
aliases: how do word parts change meaning
facts: A prefix comes at the beginning of a word or stem. A suffix comes at the end.

title: Why do some words sound alike but mean different things?
answer: Think of “pair” and “pear.” In many English accents, both words sound the same. One refers to two things and the other to a fruit. We can use the rest of the sentence to tell which word someone means. Spelling can help when we read, although some homophones are spelled alike too. Whether a pair counts as homophones can depend on the speaker’s accent. A sound difference in one place might disappear in another.

facts: “Sea” and “see” are another familiar pair of homophones in English.

title: Why does an idiom mean more than its words say?
answer: An idiom is an expression people know as a group of words. Its usual meaning can be different from what the words would describe on their own. If someone jokes that pigs can fly, the speaker probably thinks something is very unlikely. In another sentence, that same idea could be a story about a pig with wings. The surrounding words help us figure out which meaning makes sense. Idioms can change over time or be familiar to some groups and new to others.

title: What happens when two words become one idea?
answer: A compound combines two words to name one thing or idea. A “snowman” is a figure made of snow, and a “notebook” is a book for notes. You can often use what you know about the parts to guess the meaning. Still, you have to notice how the whole compound is used. A dragonfly is an insect, so the word does not mean a little dragon. Compounds may be written together, with a hyphen, or with a space between their parts.

facts: “Backpack” is a compound made from “back” and “pack.”

title: How did Sequoyah make a way to write Cherokee?
answer: Sequoyah developed signs to write the Cherokee language. Most of the signs let a reader recognize a spoken syllable at a time. Instead of learning a different mark for every word, people could learn a group of signs and use them together to write many words. Some signs look like English letters, but that does not mean they have the same sounds. The Cherokee Nation teaches the system today and uses it in materials for Cherokee language learners.

facts: Sequoyah finished developing the Cherokee syllabary in 1821.

title: Why do Korean letters fit together in blocks?
answer: Hangul is a way to write Korean. It has letters for sounds, but people arrange the letters in square-like groups. Each group represents a syllable, a small beat of speech. A syllable block can contain letters side by side and one below them. Grouping the letters helps a reader see how sounds fit together within the syllable. King Sejong helped introduce the writing system centuries ago so more people could learn a way of writing Korean.
facts: A book explaining the new writing system was published in 1446.

title: Why do Japanese readers learn three kinds of signs?
answer: A sentence in Japanese can use three sets of signs. Kanji are characters that often help show the meaning of a word. Hiragana commonly marks particles, parts added to words, or words written without kanji. Katakana can show many words borrowed from outside Japan, or draw attention to a sound or name. Hiragana and katakana both represent short units of spoken Japanese. Learning how a sentence combines the three sets can help a reader see what belongs together.

facts: Kanji originally reached Japan from China.

title: How do Arabic letters change shape in a word?
answer: Arabic writing usually runs from right to left. Many letters join their neighbors, so a letter may look somewhat different at the beginning, middle, or end of a word. A few letters do not join to the next one in that direction. Dots help tell letters with similar shapes apart. Texts for learners may add marks for short vowels, while many familiar texts leave those marks out. The shared shapes still have patterns that readers learn to recognize.

title: Why do linguists write sounds with the IPA?
answer: A word’s ordinary spelling does not always tell you how it sounds. In English, the letters “sh” work together in “ship” to spell one sound. The International Phonetic Alphabet has a separate sign for that sound. Linguists use such signs to describe speech, compare pronunciations, and write down sounds a reader might never have heard. A dictionary can use the signs to show how a word is said. Different pronunciations of one written word can get different descriptions.
facts: The IPA chart groups sounds partly by how and where we make them in the mouth or throat.

title: How did people turn plant material into paper?
answer: To make many kinds of paper, people separate plant material into tiny strands, mix them with water, and lift a thin layer on a screen. As the water drains, the strands stay in a mat. Pressing and drying make the mat into a sheet. People in China used paper early in its history, and workshops improved ways of making it over time. The idea of making light sheets from wet strands gave writers another choice besides heavier surfaces such as stone or clay.
facts: Archaeological finds show that some paper existed in China before the official Cai Lun reported improvements in 105 CE.

title: How can a printer use the same letters in different books?
answer: Movable type uses small pieces with letters or other signs on their faces. A printer sets the pieces in a frame to make lines of writing, puts ink on them, and presses them against paper. After making enough copies, the printer can take the pieces apart and arrange them to make another page. In Europe, Gutenberg’s workshop used a system like this in the 1400s. People in East Asia had made books with movable type earlier.

title: How could Gothic builders make room for tall windows?
answer: Medieval Gothic builders used pointed arches, ribs along ceilings, and strong supports outside some high walls. Together, these features helped carry the weight of the stone and reduce some of the pressure on parts of the wall. Builders could put large windows in more places. Pieces of colored glass let sunlight make different patterns during the day. The outside supports and inside stone ribs are still easy to see in many Gothic churches and cathedrals today.

facts: Gothic builders often used stone supports called flying buttresses outside tall buildings.

title: Why does a flying buttress look like a bridge beside a wall?
answer: A tall stone ceiling can push sideways on its walls as well as down. A flying buttress carries some of that sideways push away from the upper wall across an open space to a strong stone support. From a distance it looks like a short bridge to nowhere, but its job is to help hold the building steady. Often the space beneath it leaves room for paths or windows, while the broad support sends the forces down into the ground.
facts: A flying buttress connects an upper wall to a support farther away from the wall.

title: How did older cities start to build skyscrapers?
answer: In a building with heavy stone walls, the walls near the ground can become very thick as more floors are added. Builders in the late 1800s began giving tall buildings strong frames made of metal. A frame could carry more of the weight directly to the ground. That helped leave more room for windows and indoor space. Elevators also made it practical for people to reach many upper floors. Together these changes let cities fit more working space onto a piece of land.
facts: Chicago’s Home Insurance Building was an influential early tall building that opened in the 1880s.

title: Why did builders carve buildings into cliffs at Petra?
answer: Petra was a trading city of the Nabataeans in what is now Jordan. Tall sandstone cliffs surrounded it. In some places, builders carved fronts and rooms directly into the rock instead of setting blocks on top of one another. Traders reached the city along routes connecting lands across dry country. To make it possible to live there, people collected and carried water in carefully built channels and storage places. The rock buildings and waterways give different clues about the same city.

facts: A narrow passage between high rock walls leads into Petra.

title: Why was the Taj Mahal built?
answer: The Mughal ruler Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra, India, to honor his wife Mumtaz Mahal after she died. It includes a tomb, gardens, waterways, and several other structures. The large white marble building sits at one end of the garden. Its dome stands above walls decorated with stone patterns and writing. A long pool can reflect the building along a central line. These choices help visitors see how the parts of the design fit together.

title: How can dry earth become a wall?
answer: Builders can mix earth with water and shape it into adobe bricks. The bricks dry in the air and sun before people place them in a wall. A thick wall can slow the movement of heat into a room, which can be useful in a place that is hot in the day. Builders protect the outside with roof edges or layers they can repair because too much water can soften the earth again. Adobe traditions continue in many places.

title: Why do some Buddhist towers have stacked roofs?
answer: A pagoda is a tower found in parts of Asia. In many examples, each level has a wide roof or ledge that makes the tower look like a stack. Pagodas can be made of stone, wood, or brick, and the shape changes from place to place. Many were built in connection with Buddhism. A pagoda may mark a special place or hold objects important to worship. Some are mostly solid inside, even if the outside looks as if it has rooms on every level.
